To use indirect object pronouns: mi, ti, gli, le, Le, ci, vi, gli.
To tell lo / la (whom?) apart from gli / le (to whom?).
To use PIACERE in the singular and plural: mi piace, mi piacciono.
To put PIACERE in the past with ESSERE: mi è piaciuto, ti sono piaciute.
To use verbs built like PIACERE: mancare, servire, sembrare.
To choose and give a present: Che cosa gli regalo? Le piacerà?
Early March. Giulia's birthday is on the 21st of March. Matei is sitting in the trattoria kitchen with Graziella and Pietro and doesn't know what to give her.
Graziella, I have a problem. It's Giulia's birthday on the twenty-first and I don't know what to give her.
She likes art, obviously. She likes yellow flowers and Neapolitan coffee. She doesn't like waiting… but she's always late.
Give her a watch! Then she'll be on time.
Ha ha, no. A watch seems a bit unromantic to me.
Romantic? Then it's not a present for a colleague…
(red) Er… Ilinca has already sent her a birthday message. I want to give her something special.
Listen. Giulia misses Naples, doesn't she? Yesterday she told me she misses the sea.
Then go to Signor Franco's. In his shop there's a little old painting of the Bay of Naples. It's dirty and damaged, but you're a restorer, aren't you?
Graziella, you're a genius! I'll phone him right away.
And what are you giving me? My birthday's in July!
I'm giving you a watch. You need it more than Giulia does!
The pronoun "gli" is read as a soft "ly", as in "figlio": GLI te-le-FO-no = "lyee te-le-fo-no".
CC + i + o = a long "ch": PIAC-cio-no = "pyat-cho-no". The stress is on the first syllable!
Three clear vowels: au-GOO-ri. "Tanti auguri!" — stressed on GU.
Four syllables, stressed on the second-to-last: o-ro-LO-jo. GIO = "jo"; the i isn't read separately.
The indirect object answers the question "to whom?". In Italian it's introduced by "a": "telefono A Giulia" → "LE telefono" (I phone her).
Mi scrivi? (Will you write to me?)
Mi, ti, ci, vi are identical to the direct ones. The difference only shows in the 3rd person: lo / la / li / le (direct) ≠ gli / le (indirect).
Look at the verb: does it need "a" before the person? Then it's indirect.
Regalo un libro ai ragazzi. → Gli regalo un libro.
Trap: "telefonare A qualcuno" is indirect in Italian ("gli telefono"), although in Romanian we say "îl sun" (direct). But "aspettare qualcuno" is direct, as in Romanian: "la aspetto" = "o aștept".
In the passato prossimo, indirect pronouns do NOT agree: "Le ho telefonato" (not "telefonata"). Only lo / la / li / le agree.
PIACERE works exactly like Romanian "a plăcea": the thing that pleases is the subject, the person is the indirect object.
A Matei piace Firenze. = Gli piace Firenze.
A Giulia non piacciono le attese.
Not "Io piaccio il caffè"! That would mean "the coffee likes me". "Mi piaci" = "I like you" — that's what you say to someone you're in love with.
4. PIACERE in the past and future
In the passato prossimo PIACERE takes ESSERE, and the participle agrees with the thing that pleases:
"Le piacerà?" = "Will she like it?" — we'll learn the future in chapter 19, but this question is useful already.
Mi manchi. Le manca il mare.
I miss you. She misses the sea.
Ten minutes is enough for me.
"Mi manchi" = "you are missing to me" = "I miss you". The subject is the person who is missing: "Mi mancate" = "I miss you all".
Quando è il compleanno di Giulia?
L'arte, i fiori gialli e il caffè napoletano
Che cosa c'è nel negozio del signor Franco?
Un vecchio quadretto del golfo di Napoli

Signor Franco's little painting was as small as a book and as black as a frying pan. "A Neapolitan lady brought it to me thirty years ago," the old man told him. "Nobody ever wanted it. I'll give it to you, young man. You look like you're in love."

For two weeks Matei worked on it every evening in his room, when everyone was asleep. Graziella brought him camomile tea and asked him no questions. Pietro, on the other hand, asked him a hundred questions a day.
Beneath the dirt, little by little, the bay appeared: the blue sea, Vesuvius with a thread of smoke, a white boat, and on the beach two tiny figures holding hands.
Matei also cleaned the old gilded frame. On the back of the painting he found a pencil inscription, almost invisible: "Sorrento, 1953".

On the 21st of March the workshop was full of flowers. Professor Bellini gave Giulia a book on Caravaggio ("It will be useful to you," he said, as serious as ever). The colleagues sang her "Happy Birthday" in three different and slightly out-of-tune languages.

Matei waited until evening. He walked her home along the Arno, with the parcel under his arm and his heart in his mouth. In front of the green door on via dei Serragli he gave it to her without a word.

Giulia opened it. For a long moment she said nothing. Then she turned the painting over and read the inscription. "Sorrento, 1953… Matei, Grandma Assunta got married in Sorrento in 1954. She and Grandpa lived there." She looked at the two figures on the beach. "It can't be."
"It's probably not them," said Matei. "But I like to think so." Giulia hugged the painting to her chest, the way a little girl hugs her cat.
In the parcel there was also a card. Giulia read it aloud, softly: "Happy birthday. You miss the sea, I know. So I've brought you a piece of the sea. P.S.: I like you. Since October."
Giulia looked up. Her eyes were shining. "Since October?" she repeated. "Matei, you really are slow. I like you too. Since September."
And for the first time in six months, Giulia was early: she kissed him before he could say another word.
